name: Aisha Wagner

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for having me, Aisha. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no links to companies, unions, parties or government. What you tell me stays confidential. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive a front-end loader on the run-of-mine pad at a nickel mine. That's the big flat area where the trucks tip the ore, and I scoop it up and feed it into the crusher. I start at six, finish at six, and pray in the cab at lunch. I raised five children at home for thirty years, and I only came to the mine at fifty-five when my husband Karl hurt his back and had to stop working.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: So the family relies on your wage now?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Mostly, yes. Karl gets a small disability pension, but my wage is what pays the house and helps our youngest through her nursing course. I'm still learning; the crusher operator, Mick, radios me twenty times a shift to say slow down or feed more. I don't mind. Raising five children teaches you to take instructions from people who think they know best.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a relief that people still matter. At church I'd say the good Lord made us to work, and that's still true. I might share something on the family group, but mostly I'd just get on with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I can keep this job and see our youngest finish her nursing degree. Then I'd work to sixty-seven, because I started late and Karl can't work. That's the plan, and it holds in this picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep on, get better with the loader so Mick stops radioing me so much. I'd keep using the AI on my phone now and then, which my granddaughter set up, mostly to check my roster or translate letters for my mother. We'd keep putting about three hundred a month away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Grateful, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How did you start using the AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My granddaughter, who's fourteen, showed me at Easter. I watched her use it for a month before I tried it, because I wanted to see it wasn't making things up. Now I use it maybe once a week, for small things, and I always check with a person if it's important.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in this picture that would bother you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only that young people might still think hard work is old-fashioned. My grandsons want to make videos for a living. I'd rather they learned a trade, with or without AI.

S0.say: I'd say it's a relief that people still matter, and at church she'd say God made us to work. She might share something with the family group but mostly get on with it.
S0.think: It means she keeps the job and sees her youngest through nursing. She'd then work to sixty-seven, since she started late and Karl can't work.
S0.do: Keeps improving on the loader so the crusher operator needs to correct her less. Keeps using AI now and then for rosters and translating letters, and saves about three hundred a month.
S0.quote: I watched her use it for a month before I tried it, because I wanted to see it wasn't making things up.
S0.fieldNote: Aisha is the main earner since her husband's injury, which makes the job central to her family. She tested AI by watching her granddaughter for a month first, a clear sign of her steady approach. Faith and family run through everything she says.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say change has always come, and good people adjust. Work hard, learn what's needed and look after your family. But I'd also say the company should train its own people first, not just hire young ones from the city.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it worries me more than I'd show. I'm the newest on the pad, and I've seen videos of loaders that drive themselves. If my wage goes, the house goes, and our youngest might have to stop her course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd watch the first people who go through the new training, and once a few of them were doing well, I'd sign up too. I'd move another hundred a month into savings and skip the trip to see my sister in the summer. I'd talk to my eldest son about whether he could help with his sister's fees if needed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. My chest goes tight thinking about the fees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your youngest about her course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, you finish it, whatever happens. Nurses will always be needed, more than loader drivers. Even if it means I clean houses on the weekend, she's finishing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why wait for others to try the training first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've seen the company start things and drop them. When they brought in the new radio system, half of it didn't work for months. I'd let others find the problems, then I'd learn it properly.

S1.say: I'd say change always comes and good people adjust by working hard and looking after family. The company should train its own people first rather than hire young ones from the city.
S1.think: It worries her more than she'd show, because she's newest on the pad and has seen self-driving loaders. If her wage goes, the house could go and her youngest might have to stop her nursing course.
S1.do: Signs up for training once a few colleagues have done well with it. Saves another hundred a month, skips the summer trip to her sister and asks her eldest son about helping with his sister's fees.
S1.feel: Anxious, with a tight chest about the fees.
S1.quote: Even if it means I clean houses on the weekend, she's finishing.
S1.fieldNote: As the main earner, Aisha feels steady change more sharply than her calm public line suggests. Her steady approach shows again in letting others test the training first. Her daughter's nursing course is the thing she'll protect at all costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a test, and families and churches will have to carry each other. I'd say the government shouldn't just hand out money and leave people with no purpose. People need work, not just cheques.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be terrified. Two years, and my wage is gone before our youngest graduates, with Karl's small pension and maybe five months of savings. I don't know what a woman of fifty-nine who's only ever raised children and driven a loader does then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop everything except the house, food and her fees, straight away. I'd talk with my children about whether Karl and I move in with our eldest daughter, who has a big house, and rent ours out. I'd ask the church about any work going, cleaning or cooking, for as long as people still want a person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be up at night praying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would moving in with your daughter mean to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would be hard on my pride. I always thought we'd be the ones taking them in. But that's what family is for, and the grandchildren would like having us there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said people need work, not cheques. Would you take a government payment if one came?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it came, I'd take it, I'm not foolish. But I'd want to do something for it, even volunteering at the school. Taking money for nothing would sit badly with me.

S2.say: I'd say it's a test, and families and churches will have to carry each other. The government shouldn't just hand out money and leave people with no purpose.
S2.think: She'd be terrified, with her wage gone before her youngest graduates and only Karl's small pension and about five months of savings. She doesn't know what work there'd be for her at fifty-nine.
S2.do: Cuts spending to the house, food and her daughter's fees straight away. Considers moving in with her eldest daughter and renting out their house, and asks the church about cleaning or cooking work.
S2.quote: I always thought we'd be the ones taking them in.
S2.fieldNote: With her as the main earner, the two-year picture threatens the whole household. Her traditional values come through in turning to family and church first. She'd accept a government payment but would want to give something back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is time to prepare properly. Families should sit down and plan. I'd tell the young ones at work to learn a trade that needs hands, like electrics.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be sixty-three, not sixty-seven. So I'd miss four years of the wages I was counting on. But our youngest would be qualified by then, which takes the biggest weight off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save hard for five years, aiming to have a year saved by 2030. I'd do the training on the new automated loaders once it's working for others. And Karl and I would talk about selling the house and moving somewhere smaller, closer to our children, before prices change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I'd feel I could plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut to save hard?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The Sunday lunches out after church, the new car we'd talked about, and some of the presents for the grandchildren. I'd still give to the church, though. That's not negotiable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do the extra years change compared with the fast one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly my daughter. In two years she'd be halfway through her course. In five, she's a nurse with her own wage. That's the difference between panic and worry.

S3.say: I'd say five years is time for families to sit down and plan. She'd tell young workers to learn a hands-on trade like electrics.
S3.think: She'd be sixty-three, losing four years of wages she was counting on. But her youngest would be qualified, which lifts the biggest weight.
S3.do: Saves hard towards a year's cushion by 2030 and trains on the automated loaders once they work for others. With Karl, considers selling up and moving to a smaller place nearer their children.
S3.quote: That's the difference between panic and worry.
S3.fieldNote: For Aisha, timing comes down to her daughter graduating. She'd cut spending but keep giving to the church, which shows her priorities. Her plan combines steady saving, proven training and a family move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time for sensible people. I'd tell my grandsons to get a trade and stop making videos. I'd keep my opinions for the family table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be sixty-eight, just after I'd planned to stop. So I'd be cutting it close, but I'd probably make it. If they started trimming early, though, the junior ones go first, and that's me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep on, get better on the loader and do the automation training once it's proven. I'd keep saving the same. And I'd push my grandsons towards apprenticeships, maybe even pay for a welding course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, more than calm. Close enough to the finish that a slip would hurt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you feel safer in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Knowing the company would keep its older workers to the end of their time. A promise in writing, not just words at a meeting. I've learned that promises at meetings blow away like dust on the pad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you pay for the welding course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, if he'd go. Maybe five hundred dollars towards it. I'd rather spend that than see him on the couch making videos at twenty-five.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is plenty for sensible people, and she'd push her grandsons towards a trade. She'd keep her views for the family table.
S4.think: She'd be sixty-eight, just after her planned retirement at sixty-seven, so it's close but she'd probably make it. If cuts started early, though, she's junior and would go first.
S4.do: Keeps working, improves on the loader and does automation training once it's proven. Keeps saving the same and offers about five hundred dollars towards a welding course for her grandson.
S4.feel: More uneasy than calm, close enough to the finish that a slip would hurt.
S4.quote: I've learned that promises at meetings blow away like dust on the pad.
S4.fieldNote: Because she started late and needs to work to sixty-seven, even ten years leaves her close to the line. She wants written guarantees, not spoken ones. Her family focus moves to her grandsons and apprenticeships.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. My wage would go before my daughter finishes, and Karl can't work. What would help is the company keeping older workers on until the pension, in writing, and some help for families with children still studying.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what my family thinks of me working in a mine. My sons were embarrassed at first. Now they brag about their mother driving a loader the size of a house, and I'd like to keep giving them something to brag about.

headlineQuote: Now they brag about their mother driving a loader the size of a house, and I'd like to keep giving them something to brag about.
portrait: Aisha Wagner is a fifty-eight-year-old mother of five who raised her children at home and only started driving a front-end loader at a nickel mine at fifty-five, after her husband Karl hurt his back. Her wage is now the family's main income and pays for her youngest daughter's nursing course. She's a woman of faith who believes in work and family over handouts, and she tries new technology like AI only once she's seen it work for others. She's calm if AI fizzles but anxious with steady change, alarmed by AGI in two years, and still uneasy with ten years because she planned to work to sixty-seven.
biggestWorry: AGI in two years worries her most, because her wage would disappear before her daughter finishes nursing and Karl can't work.
whatWouldHelp: A written promise from the company to keep older workers on until the pension, and help for families with children still studying.
